Region: Nile Valley, northeast Africa
History: Unified under the pharaohs around 3100 BC, Egypt endured through the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms, building an empire that stretched into Canaan and Nubia. It later fell to Assyria, Persia, Greece, and Rome, but its monuments and records outlasted every conqueror.
Culture: Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs, built pyramids and temples on a monumental scale, and advanced medicine, astronomy, and administration. The annual Nile flood made farming predictable and supported one of the ancient world's most stable states.
Religion: Egypt worshipped many gods, chief among them Ra, Osiris, Isis, and Horus, and treated the pharaoh as a divine king. Belief in judgment after death shaped its tombs, mummification, and funerary texts.
BibleConnection: Abraham visited Egypt in famine; Joseph rose to vizier there; Israel spent centuries in Egypt before the Exodus, the defining deliverance of the Old Testament. Later kings allied with Egypt, refugees fled there after Jerusalem's fall, and Joseph and Mary took the infant Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Miriam; Zipporah; Mizraim
RelatedEvents: Abram in Egypt; Joseph and His Brothers; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Region: Eastern Mediterranean coast and hill country, between Egypt and Mesopotamia
History: Canaan was a land of independent city-states rather than one empire, fought over by Egypt and Mesopotamia. God promised it to Abraham's descendants, and under Joshua Israel conquered and settled it, then struggled for generations to hold it against its peoples.
Culture: Canaanites farmed, traded, and built walled cities, and wrote in an early alphabet that influenced later scripts. Their pottery, idols, and fortifications appear throughout the archaeology of Israel.
Religion: Canaanite religion centered on El and Baal, with Asherah and ritual practices Scripture repeatedly condemns, including child sacrifice. Israel's recurring turn to Baal worship is one of the Old Testament's persistent warnings.
BibleConnection: Canaan is the Promised Land of the patriarchs, the land of the conquest under Joshua, and the setting of Judges. Its peoples and gods are the constant test of Israel's faithfulness to the covenant.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; Jacob; Joshua; Rahab; Caleb; Melchizedek
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Walls of Jericho; Crossing the Jordan

Region: Southern coastal plain of Canaan: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath
History: The Philistines were part of the Sea Peoples who settled the coast around 1200 BC, organized in a league of five cities. They fought Israel from the days of the judges through David, captured the ark briefly, and were eventually absorbed by the empires that followed.
Culture: Philistine pottery, iron-working, and Aegean roots set them apart from their Canaanite neighbors. Their cities were wealthy trading ports ruled by lords called serens.
Religion: The Philistines worshipped Dagon, Ashtoreth, and Baal-zebub. The ark's capture and Dagon's fall before it (1 Samuel 5) became a vivid sign of God's supremacy over their gods.
BibleConnection: Philistia is the great rival of Israel's early history: Samson's enemy, the home of Goliath, and the power David fought before and after becoming king. The word Palestine derives from Philistia.
RelatedEvents: Samson and Delilah; David and Goliath

Region: Northern Levantine coast: Tyre, Sidon, Byblos
History: Phoenician city-states dominated Mediterranean trade, founding colonies as far as Carthage. They were never a single empire, but their ships, timber, and purple dye made them indispensable partners of Israel's kings.
Culture: Phoenicians are credited with spreading the alphabet that became the ancestor of Greek and Latin scripts. Their cedar timber built temples and palaces across the region.
Religion: Phoenician religion honored Baal, Astarte, and Eshmun, with rites Scripture condemns. Jezebel, daughter of Sidon's king, brought Baal worship to Israel's court with devastating effect.
BibleConnection: Hiram of Tyre supplied cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's temple; Jezebel's marriage to Ahab imported Baal worship; Jesus visited the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Syrophoenician woman's faith drew his praise.

Region: Syria, centered on Damascus
History: Aramean kingdoms, chiefly Damascus, rose after the Bronze Age collapse and contested the land east and north of Israel. Aram fought Israel under Ben-Hadad and Hazael, allied with it at times, and finally fell to Assyria in 732 BC.
Culture: Aramaic, the language of the Arameans, became the lingua franca of the Near East and the everyday language of Jesus' world. Aramean trade and diplomacy connected Mesopotamia with the Levant.
Religion: Arameans worshipped Hadad (Rimmon), the storm god, among others. Naaman, commander of Aram's army, was healed of leprosy after washing in the Jordan at Elisha's word.
BibleConnection: Aram is both enemy and neighbor in Kings: wars with Ahab and Jehoram, the siege of Samaria, and Naaman's healing, which showed God's mercy reaching beyond Israel.

Region: Highlands east of the Dead Sea
History: Moab, descended from Lot according to Genesis, was a small kingdom east of the Dead Sea that alternated between war and uneasy peace with Israel. King Mesha's revolt against Israel is recorded both in 2 Kings 3 and on his own victory stele.
Culture: Moabites farmed the highlands and controlled the King's Highway trade route. Their language was closely related to Hebrew, and their royal inscriptions are among the closest parallels to biblical Hebrew.
Religion: Moab worshipped Chemosh, to whom kings offered sacrifices, including, at least once, a king's own son in wartime desperation. Ruth the Moabitess, who left Moab to follow Naomi's God, became an ancestor of David.
BibleConnection: Balak of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel; Ruth came from Moab; and the plains of Moab are where Moses died within sight of the Promised Land.
RelatedPeople: Ruth; Naomi; Boaz; Lot; Balaam; Balak
RelatedFinds: Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone); Balaam Inscription (Deir Alla Inscription)

Region: East of the Jordan, around modern Amman
History: The Ammonites, descended from Lot's son Ben-Ammi, held the land east of the Jordan around their capital Rabbah. They clashed with Israel from the judges through David, who captured Rabbah, and survived as a small state into the Persian period.
Culture: Ammon shared the language and material culture of its neighbors Moab and Israel, and its capital Rabbah was a fortified trade center on the King's Highway.
Religion: Ammon worshipped Molech (Milcom), whose rites included child sacrifice, which the Law of Moses strictly forbade. Solomon's Ammonite wives brought Molech's worship into Jerusalem itself.
BibleConnection: Jephthah defeated Ammon; Saul's first victory as king was against Ammon's siege of Jabesh-gilead; David's war with Ammon frames the Bathsheba story.

Region: South of the Dead Sea, from the Arabah to the Red Sea
History: Edom, descended from Esau, occupied the rugged land south of the Dead Sea and controlled the copper mines of the Arabah and the Red Sea port of Ezion-geber. Edom refused Israel passage in the wilderness, warred with Judah's kings, and was later displaced by the Nabataeans; its people, the Idumeans, included Herod the Great's family.
Culture: Edomites built their capital at Bozrah and the mountain stronghold of Petra's region, living by mining, herding, and tolls on the trade routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean.
Religion: Edom worshipped Qos as its chief god. The prophet Obadiah pronounced judgment on Edom for standing by, and even joining in, when Jerusalem fell.
BibleConnection: Edom is Esau's land, the brother-nation that became Israel's rival: the birthright story, the refused passage, and Obadiah's oracle all turn on that brotherhood.

Region: Anatolia (modern Turkey), with influence into Syria and Canaan
History: The Hittites built one of the Bronze Age's great empires from their capital Hattusa, fighting Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and concluding the earliest surviving peace treaty. After the empire's fall around 1200 BC, smaller Neo-Hittite states survived in Syria for centuries.
Culture: Hittites pioneered iron-working, codified laws, and drew up detailed treaties and covenants. Their treaty forms — preamble, history, stipulations, blessings and curses — closely parallel the structure of the biblical covenants.
Religion: Hittite religion embraced a thousand gods, led by the storm god Tarhunt and the sun goddess Arinna. Their rituals and legal texts show a world of oaths, purity rules, and treaty obligations.
BibleConnection: Hittites appear in the patriarchal stories: Ephron the Hittite sold Abraham the cave of Machpelah, and Uriah the Hittite was the husband of Bathsheba. Hittite treaty patterns help explain the shape of God's covenants with Israel.

Region: Northern Mesopotamia, capital Nineveh
History: Assyria rose from a city-state on the Tigris to the Near East's first true empire, conquering the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and deporting its people. Its siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC failed, and Nineveh itself fell to Babylon and Media in 612 BC.
Culture: Assyrians built vast palaces and libraries — Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh — and administered their empire with roads, officials, and mass deportations.
Religion: Assyria's chief god was Assur, with Ishtar of Nineveh and other gods of war and fertility. Its kings presented conquest as divine mandate, and their annals record cruelty as policy.
BibleConnection: Assyria is the rod of God's judgment in Isaiah and the repentant city of Jonah's preaching. Its fall, celebrated by Nahum, showed that even the mightiest empire answers to God.
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion; Fall of Samaria
RelatedFinds: Sennacherib Prism (Taylor Prism); Lachish Reliefs; Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III; Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III

Region: Southern Mesopotamia, capital Babylon
History: Babylon, heir of Sumer and Akkad, reached its height under Hammurabi and again under Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC and carried Judah into exile. Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BC without a battle.
Culture: Babylon gave the world Hammurabi's law code, advanced astronomy and mathematics, the Hanging Gardens tradition, and the ziggurat — the stepped temple tower behind the Babel story.
Religion: Babylon worshipped Marduk above a large pantheon, with Ishtar, Shamash, and Nabu among the chief gods. Its priests read omens in the stars and livers, a practice Daniel's God repeatedly overruled.
BibleConnection: Babylon is both a place and a symbol in Scripture: the tower of Babel, the exile that reshaped Israel's faith, Daniel's court, and the 'Babylon' of Revelation standing for every proud power opposed to God.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Daniel in the Lions' Den
RelatedFinds: Babylonian Chronicle (Nebuchadnezzar's Chronicle); Code of Hammurabi; Nabonidus Cylinder; Jehoiachin's Rations Tablets; Al-Yahudu Tablets

Region: Iran plateau to the Mediterranean, capital Susa and Persepolis
History: Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire, the largest the ancient world had yet seen, stretching from India to Greece. His edict let the Jewish exiles return and rebuild the temple; later kings Darius, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes framed the world of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther.
Culture: Persia administered its empire through satrapies, royal roads, and a policy of tolerance toward local customs and gods. Its postal system and coinage knit together peoples from three continents.
Religion: Persian kings promoted Ahura Mazda, the wise lord of Zoroastrian teaching, while tolerating the religions of their subjects. The empire's tolerance is what made the return from exile possible.
BibleConnection: Persia is the setting of the return: Cyrus's decree, the temple's rebuilding, Esther in Susa, and Nehemiah's wall. Isaiah calls Cyrus God's anointed, the pagan king who serves God's purpose.
RelatedPeople: Cyrus the Great; Mordecai; Nehemiah; Ezra; Elam
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Esther Saves Her People; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple; Ezra Reads the Law

Region: Greek mainland, Aegean islands, and Alexander's eastern empire
History: Greek city-states gave the West philosophy, drama, and democracy, and Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture across the East. After Alexander, his successors ruled the world of the Maccabees, and Greek became the language in which the New Testament was written.
Culture: Greece prized reason, rhetoric, athletics, and art, and its language became the common tongue of the eastern Mediterranean. The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, carried Scripture to the wider world.
Religion: Greeks worshipped Zeus, Athena, Apollo, and a host of gods on Olympus and in every city. Paul found Athens full of idols and an altar 'to an unknown god,' which became his opening to preach Christ.
BibleConnection: Daniel foresaw Greece as the goat that shatters Persia's ram; the New Testament was written in Greek; and Paul's missionary journeys carried the gospel through the Greek cities of Corinth, Athens, Philippi, and Ephesus.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; The Conversion of Paul
RelatedFinds: Gallio Inscription; Corinth Bema (Judgment Seat); Politarch Inscription; Erastus Inscription

Region: Italian peninsula to an empire around the Mediterranean
History: Rome grew from a city-state to a republic and then an empire that ruled the whole Mediterranean world, including Judea from 63 BC. Its roads, laws, and peace — the Pax Romana — form the backdrop of the entire New Testament.
Culture: Rome built roads, aqueducts, and cities on a scale never seen before, spread Latin law and citizenship, and absorbed Greek art and learning. Its engineering and administration held a vast empire together for centuries.
Religion: Romans worshipped Jupiter, Mars, and the emperor himself, whose cult demanded loyalty from every subject. Christians' refusal to call Caesar lord was one reason for their persecution.
BibleConnection: Jesus was born under Caesar Augustus's census, crucified under Pontius Pilate, and Paul appealed to Caesar and was imprisoned in Rome itself. The empire that killed the apostles also carried their message to the ends of the earth.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; Paul in Rome
RelatedFinds: Pilate Stone; Herodium (Herod's Tomb); Ephesus Theater; Sergius Paulus Inscription

Region: Alexandria, Egypt
History: Alexandria was the great Hellenistic city of Egypt, founded by Alexander. Men of the synagogue of the Alexandrians disputed with Stephen, and Apollos, eloquent in the Scriptures, came from Alexandria to Ephesus.
Culture: A centre of learning and philosophy, and home of Greek-speaking Judaism — the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, was produced there.
Religion: A large Jewish community alongside pagan temples; Alexandrian Judaism shaped the Greek-speaking church.
BibleConnection: Alexandrians appear as Stephen's disputants and as the home community of Apollos, whose preaching Paul and Priscilla and Aquila corrected and encouraged.

TimePeriod: c. 2000-700 BC, from Abraham's day to Hezekiah's reign
Region: The Negev, the Sinai wilderness, and the southern borders of Canaan, ranging at times into the hill country
History: The Amalekites appear as early as Genesis 14:7, in the days of Abraham, and Genesis 36:12 traces Amalek to Eliphaz son of Esau. They attacked Israel at Rephidim after the exodus (Exodus 17:8-16), where Moses' raised hands decided the battle; Balaam's oracle called Amalek 'the first of the nations' (Numbers 24:20); and Deuteronomy 25:17-19 commanded Israel to remember how they struck the stragglers and to blot out their remembrance. Saul's failure to destroy them cost him the kingdom (1 Samuel 15), David destroyed the raiders who burned Ziklag (1 Samuel 30), and a remnant was wiped out in Hezekiah's days (1 Chronicles 4:43).
Culture: Nomadic raiders of the southern desert, striking the weak and the rear of a marching people, then vanishing into the wilderness. They lived by plunder rather than by cities.
Religion: The text describes no Amalekite religion in detail; their defining mark in the Bible is hostility to Israel, from Rephidim to Haman's later line (Esther 3:1 traces Haman to Agag).
BibleConnection: Amalek is Israel's standing enemy: the first nation to make war on Israel after the exodus, the test of Saul's obedience, and the target of David's vengeance at Ziklag.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 14:7; Exodus 17:8-16; Numbers 24:20; Deuteronomy 25:17-19; 1 Samuel 15:1-9; 1 Samuel 30:1-18
RelatedPeople: Moses; Joshua; King Saul; King David; Amalek; Esau
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Region: The hill country of Canaan and Transjordan, including the kingdoms of Sihon at Heshbon and Og at Bashan
History: The Amorites were one of the major peoples of Canaan. In Genesis 15:16 the LORD tells Abram that his descendants will return to the land when 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full,' naming the Amorites for the land's peoples as a whole. In Numbers 21, Sihon king of the Amorites refused Israel passage and was defeated, and Og king of Bashan was defeated likewise, giving Israel its first Transjordan territory. Amos 2:9-10 recalls them as a people tall as cedars and strong as oaks, destroyed before Israel. Amorite names also appear widely in Mesopotamian records of the period.
Culture: A Semitic people who moved from a pastoral life into cities and kingdoms across the Levant and Mesopotamia. In Canaan they held fortified hill-country towns and, east of the Jordan, organized kingdoms with kings, armies, and walled cities such as Heshbon.
Religion: They shared the religious world of Bronze Age Canaan, worshipping the gods of the Canaanite pantheon. The Bible presents their worship as part of the idolatry Israel was commanded to reject.
BibleConnection: The Amorites are the standing example of the peoples whose land Israel inherited: named in the promise to Abram, defeated in the wilderness, listed among the seven nations to be driven out, and remembered by the prophets as proof of God's judgment and gift.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 15:16; Genesis 15:21; Numbers 21:21-35; Deuteronomy 1:27; Deuteronomy 7:1; Amos 2:9-10
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

TimePeriod: Wilderness and conquest era, c. 1400-1200 BC
Region: The hill country of Judah (Hebron, Debir, Anab) and, after the conquest, Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod
History: The Anakim descended from Anak (Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 9:2). The spies reported them as giants: 'we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight' (Numbers 13:33). Joshua cut them off from the hill country, leaving a remnant only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod (Joshua 11:21-22). Caleb drove out Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak, from Hebron (Joshua 15:13-14), and Judges 1:20 records Caleb's taking of Hebron from the three sons of Anak.
Culture: A tall, formidable hill people whose walled towns and stature terrified the spies. Their cities in the hill country were the strongholds Caleb claimed by faith.
Religion: No distinct Anakim religion is described; they belong to the Canaanite world whose idolatry Israel was told to reject.
BibleConnection: The Anakim are the giants of the spies' report and of Caleb's faith: the very people Israel feared became the inheritance of the one spy who trusted God.
KeyScriptures: Numbers 13:28; Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 9:2; Joshua 11:21-22; Joshua 15:13-14; Judges 1:20
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Region: The Arabian Peninsula and the Syrian desert fringe
History: Arabians were the nomadic herders and caravan traders of the desert between Mesopotamia and Egypt. Kings of Arabia brought tribute to Solomon (1 Kings 10:15), Arabians raided Judah in Jehoram's reign (2 Chronicles 21:16) and joined the opposition to Nehemiah's wall under Geshem the Arabian (Nehemiah 2:19; 4:7), and Arabians were among the peoples who heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:11). Paul went away into Arabia after his conversion (Galatians 1:17).
Culture: Arabians lived by herding and by the caravan trade in incense, spices, and goods moving between Yemen, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean, organized in tribes under sheikhs.
Religion: Arabians worshipped pre-Islamic deities of the desert, including Al-Lat and Al-Uzza, alongside the astral gods of the caravan cities.
BibleConnection: Isaiah's oracle, the burden upon Arabia (Isaiah 21:13), and Jeremiah's list of Arabia's kings (Jeremiah 25:24) set Arabia among the nations judged with Judah's neighbors, while Pentecost and Paul's journey make Arabia part of the gospel's early geography.
KeyScriptures: 1 Kings 10:15; Isaiah 21:13; Jeremiah 25:24; Ezekiel 27:21; Nehemiah 2:19; Acts 2:11; Galatians 1:17

Region: Canaan (later Arka, on the Phoenician coast, is the common identification)
History: The Arkites are named in the Table of Nations as descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:17; 1 Chronicles 1:15), with no further biblical history. The later Phoenician coastal town of Arka in northern Lebanon is commonly identified with them, but the text itself does not make that connection.
Culture: Nothing is recorded of Arkite culture beyond their place in the Canaanite family list; the later Arka was a Phoenician coastal town.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Arkite religion.
BibleConnection: The Arkites appear only in the Table of Nations, one branch of Canaan's family spread abroad after Babel.

Region: The island city of Arvad, off the Phoenician coast
History: The Arvadites, descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:18; 1 Chronicles 1:16), were the people of Arvad, an island city off the Phoenician coast. Ezekiel pictures Arvad's men as Tyre's mariners and as soldiers on Tyre's walls (Ezekiel 27:8, 11) — seafarers in the service of the great trading city.
Culture: Arvadites were seafarers and shipbuilders, manning Tyre's fleets and garrisoning its walls.
Religion: As a Phoenician city, Arvad shared the religion of the Phoenician coast; nothing distinct is recorded of Arvadite worship.
BibleConnection: Arvad's biblical footprint is maritime: the island people whose sailors and soldiers powered Tyre's trade and defense.

Region: Northern Mediterranean coast, from Carmel toward Tyre and Sidon
History: Asher was Jacob's eighth son, by Leah's servant Zilpah. His name means happy, and Jacob blessed him with rich food and royal delicacies (Genesis 49:20). Asher's allotment ran along the northern coast, but the tribe never drove out the Canaanites of its towns (Judges 1:31-32) and lived among them. Asher is the quietest tribe in the history: it appears in the census lists and in the blessing of Moses (Deuteronomy 33:24-25), and Anna the prophetess, who recognised the infant Jesus in the temple, was of the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36). The tribe was deported with the northern kingdom.
Culture: Asher's culture was coastal: farming the fertile plain, trading with the Phoenician cities to its north, and living alongside Canaanite neighbours its armies never displaced.
Religion: Asher shared Israel's worship of the LORD, though living among Canaanite towns exposed it to the idolatry the conquest was meant to remove.
BibleConnection: Asher's story is one of quiet persistence: a tribe that never produced a judge or a king, yet is named among the sealed in Revelation 7 and gives the New Testament its aged prophetess Anna.
RelatedPeople: Asher; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Serah; Beriah; Heber; Anna the Prophetess

Region: Ava, in Mesopotamia
History: The Avites were one of the Mesopotamian peoples Assyria resettled in Samaria after Israel's fall (2 Kings 17:24). They made Nibhaz and Tartak their gods (2 Kings 17:31). They are not the Avvim of Deuteronomy 2:23, a different people near Gaza displaced by the Caphtorim — the similar names cover two different groups.
Culture: As a Mesopotamian people, the Avites shared the urban culture of Babylon's world; nothing further is recorded of them.
Religion: The Avites worshipped Nibhaz and Tartak, gods they carried with them to Samaria.
BibleConnection: The Avites appear only in the resettlement list and its note on their gods — one more strand in the mixed population that became Samaria.

Region: The southwestern coastal plain around Gaza, in unwalled settlements (Hazerim)
History: The Avvim dwelt in Hazerim, unwalled villages, on the coastal plain toward Gaza, until the Caphtorim came out of Caphtor, destroyed them, and dwelt in their place (Deuteronomy 2:23). Joshua 13:3 still counts the Avvim among the land yet to be taken, listed beside the five lords of the Philistines, a sign that a remnant remained into the conquest era.
Culture: Villagers of the coastal plain, living in unwalled settlements rather than fortified cities, which left them exposed to the Caphtorim who displaced them.
Religion: Not described in the text.
BibleConnection: The Avvim are a small, displaced people of the coast: an example in Deuteronomy 2 of how peoples rose and fell in the land before Israel ever arrived.

Region: The central hill country between Judah and Ephraim, including Jerusalem's northern approach
History: Benjamin was Jacob's youngest son, by Rachel, who died bearing him; Jacob called him son of his right hand (Genesis 35:18), and Moses' blessing pictured him dwelling safely beside the LORD (Deuteronomy 33:12). Benjamin's small allotment sat between Judah and Ephraim and included Jerusalem's northern approaches, Gibeah, Mizpah, and Bethel. The tribe nearly destroyed itself in the civil war over Gibeah (Judges 19–21). Saul, Israel's first king, was a Benjamite, and after the kingdom divided Benjamin stayed with Judah. Paul the apostle was of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5).
Culture: Benjamin's culture was that of a small, fierce border tribe: its men were famed as left-handed slingers and archers, and its towns guarded the passes between north and south.
Religion: Benjamin shared Israel's worship of the LORD, and its territory held some of Israel's oldest sanctuaries, including Bethel and, later, the Jerusalem temple on its border with Judah.
BibleConnection: Benjamin's story runs from near-annihilation to the apostle to the Gentiles: the smallest tribe gave Israel its first king and, centuries later, Paul.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 35:18; Genesis 49:27; Deuteronomy 33:12; Joshua 18:11-28; Judges 20:1-3; 1 Samuel 9:1-2; Philippians 3:5
RelatedPeople: Benjamin; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Jonathan; King Saul; Ehud, Son of Gera; Mordecai; Queen Esther; Paul; Kish, Son of Abiel

Region: Caphtor (commonly identified with Crete) and, after migration, the Gaza coast
History: The Caphtorim descended from Mizraim in the table of nations (Genesis 10:14). Deuteronomy 2:23 records their migration: 'the Caphtorims, which came forth out of Caphtor, destroyed the Avvims, which dwelt in Hazerim, even unto Azzah, and dwelt in their stead.' Jeremiah 47:4 calls the Philistines 'the remnant of the country of Caphtor,' and Amos 9:7 says God brought the Philistines from Caphtor as He brought Israel from Egypt. The Caphtorim are thus closely linked to Philistine origins, but they are distinct from the Philistines themselves in the Genesis 10 list, where the Philistim come from the Casluhim. Caphtor is usually identified with Crete.
Culture: A seafaring people of Caphtor who migrated to the Gaza coast and displaced its villagers, bringing Aegean connections to the coastal plain.
Religion: No distinct Caphtorim religion is described; their Philistine kin worshipped Dagon and other coastal gods.
BibleConnection: The Caphtorim explain how the Gaza coast changed hands before Israel arrived, and Amos uses their migration as a mirror of Israel's own exodus.

Region: Eastern Asia Minor (Cappadocia)
History: Cappadocia was an inland region of Asia Minor, a Roman province by New Testament times. Cappadocians are named among the hearers at Pentecost, and Peter addresses his first letter to believers scattered through Cappadocia.
Culture: A rural, volcanic plateau; Greek-speaking under Roman rule, with Persian-era roots in its older history.
Religion: Pagan cults before conversion; by the time of 1 Peter there were Christian communities scattered through the region.
BibleConnection: Named among the peoples who heard the apostles at Pentecost, and named again among the recipients of 1 Peter.

Region: Southeastern Asia Minor (Cilicia)
History: Cilicia was the coastal region of southeastern Asia Minor, home of Tarsus. Men from the synagogue of the Cilicians disputed with Stephen, and Paul — a Cilician by birth — travelled through Cilicia strengthening the churches.
Culture: Greek-Roman cities; Tarsus was a noted centre of learning, and Paul calls himself a citizen of no mean city.
Religion: Pagan cults alongside a Jewish community strong enough to have its own synagogue in Jerusalem.
BibleConnection: Cilicians appear as Stephen's disputants and as Paul's home people; the letter of the Jerusalem Council was addressed to the brethren in Cilicia as well as Syria.

Region: Island of Crete
History: Crete was a large Mediterranean island under Roman rule. Cretans are named among the hearers at Pentecost; Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every city, and his ship to Rome sheltered at the island.
Culture: Seafaring islanders; Paul quotes a Cretan prophet's proverb about Cretans, which he applies to the false teachers troubling the island's churches.
Religion: Pagan cults before conversion; by Titus's time there were churches in every Cretan city needing elders.
BibleConnection: Cretans appear at Pentecost and as the people among whom Titus worked; Paul's letter to Titus is written to that island mission.

Region: Upper Nile, south of Egypt (modern Sudan)
History: Cush, son of Ham (Genesis 10:6) and father of Nimrod, is the biblical name for the Nubian kingdom the Greeks called Ethiopia. Kushite kings ruled Egypt as its Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and Cush appears throughout the prophets as a distant southern nation. The Ethiopian eunuch baptized by Philip (Acts 8) shows Cushites still traveling to Jerusalem to worship in the New Testament period. In English Bibles the people of Cush are also called the Ethiopians.
Culture: Kushites built pyramids at Meroe, worked iron, and traded gold, ivory, ebony, and exotic goods up the Nile to Egypt and beyond.
Religion: Kushites worshipped Amun and other gods of the Nile valley, with great temples at Napata and Meroe blending Egyptian and Nubian religion.
BibleConnection: From Nimrod's kingdom to the psalmist's promise that Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands to God (Psalms 68:31), Cush stands for the far south brought within God's reach — a theme completed when Philip baptizes the Ethiopian court official.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 10:6; Psalms 68:31; Isaiah 18:1; Isaiah 43:3; Ezekiel 29:10; Acts 8:27

Region: Mesopotamia (exact site debated)
History: Cuthah was one of the Mesopotamian peoples Assyria resettled in Samaria after Israel's fall (2 Kings 17:24). The men of Cuth made Nergal their god (2 Kings 17:30). Later Jewish tradition called the Samaritans Cuthites or Cutheans after them, though the biblical text itself does not use that name for the Samaritans.
Culture: As a Mesopotamian people, the men of Cuth shared the urban, scribal, and idol-making culture of Babylon's world.
Religion: The men of Cuth worshipped Nergal, god of the underworld and of plague, whom they set up in Samaria.
BibleConnection: Cuthah's biblical footprint is the resettlement: a foreign people planted in Israel's empty cities, whose god Nergal joined the mixed worship of the new Samaria.

Region: Island of Cyprus
History: Cyprus was a Mediterranean island under Roman rule. Barnabas was a Cypriot by birth; men of Cyprus were among the first to preach to Greeks at Antioch; and Paul's first missionary journey began on Cyprus.
Culture: Greek-speaking islanders; Cyprus was famed for copper, from which it takes its name.
Religion: Pagan temples alongside a Jewish community; early Christian preaching reached the island on the first journey.
BibleConnection: Barnabas's homeland; Cyprus was evangelised at the start of the first missionary journey, and Cypriot believers helped found the church at Antioch.

Region: Cyrenaica, North Africa (Cyrene)
History: Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Cyrenians are named among the hearers at Pentecost; Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry Jesus' cross; and men of Cyrene preached to Greeks at Antioch.
Culture: A Greek city with a strong Jewish community, closely tied to Alexandria and to Jerusalem.
Religion: A Jewish synagogue community; Cyrenian believers were among the founders of the Gentile church at Antioch.
BibleConnection: Simon of Cyrene's part in the crucifixion and the Cyrenians' preaching at Antioch are their main New Testament appearances.

Region: Originally the central coastal plain; later the far north at Laish (Dan)
History: Dan was Jacob's fifth son, by Rachel's servant Bilhah. Jacob's blessing pictured Dan as a serpent by the roadside (Genesis 49:17). The tribe's first allotment on the coastal plain proved too small and too exposed, so part of the tribe migrated north and captured Laish, renaming it Dan (Judges 18) — the town that became proverbial as Israel's northern border, 'from Dan to Beersheba'. Samson, Israel's most famous judge, was a Danite. Under Jeroboam, Dan became one of the two sites of a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-30). The tribe was deported with the northern kingdom by Assyria. Dan is the one tribe absent from the sealing list in Revelation 7.
Culture: Danite culture combined coastal farming with the frontier life of a border tribe; its northern city guarded the road into Israel from Syria, and its southern settlements lived among the Philistines.
Religion: Dan shared Israel's worship of the LORD, but its history is marked by two corruptions of it: Micah's shrine with its Levite priest (Judges 17–18) and Jeroboam's golden calf at Dan, which the prophets condemned.
BibleConnection: Dan illustrates both halves of the judges period: a deliverer in Samson and, in the same tribe's story, the spread of idolatry from Micah's household shrine to a royal sanctuary.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 30:6; Genesis 49:16-17; Judges 13:2; Judges 18:1-2; Judges 18:27-29; 1 Kings 12:28-30
RelatedPeople: Dan; Jacob; Samson; Delilah; Manoah, Father of Samson; Aholiab

Region: Southwestern Iran, east of Mesopotamia, around Susa
History: One of the ancient world's oldest kingdoms, Elam lay east of Babylon with its chief city at Susa. Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, led the coalition Abraham defeated to rescue Lot (Genesis 14). Elam later warred with Assyria, was absorbed into the Persian Empire, and Susa became a Persian royal capital. Elamites were among the peoples present at Pentecost.
Culture: Elamites spoke their own language, unrelated to Semitic or Indo-European tongues, built ziggurats and palaces at Susa, and traded across Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau.
Religion: Elamites worshipped their own gods, chief among them Inshushinak, god of Susa, alongside a wider Mesopotamian pantheon.
BibleConnection: Beyond Chedorlaomer, Elam appears in judgment oracles (Isaiah 21:2; Jeremiah 49:34-39, which also promises a later restoration), in Ezekiel's lament over fallen nations, and in Daniel's vision, which takes place at Shushan in the province of Elam (Daniel 8:2).
KeyScriptures: Genesis 14:1; Isaiah 21:2; Jeremiah 49:34; Ezekiel 32:24; Daniel 8:2; Acts 2:9

Region: The plain later held by Moab, east of the Dead Sea
History: The Emim were an ancient people of the Moabite plain, remembered as giants. Chedorlaomer defeated them at Shaveh Kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5), and Deuteronomy 2:10-11 explains that the Emim 'were a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; which also were accounted giants, as the Anakims.' The Moabites, descended from Lot, inherited the land the Emim had held.
Culture: Known only as a great and tall people of the plain, counted among the Rephaim in Deuteronomy's reckoning.
Religion: Not described in the text.
BibleConnection: The Emim belong to Deuteronomy's lesson that the land's history is a history of displacements: giants held Moab's plain before Moab, just as the Anakim held Canaan before Israel.

Region: Central hill country, Shechem and Shiloh
History: Ephraim was Joseph's younger son, adopted by Jacob as a full tribal ancestor (Genesis 48). Jacob deliberately crossed his hands to bless Ephraim above his elder brother Manasseh (Genesis 48:17-20). Ephraim's allotment covered the central hill country, including Shechem and Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood. Joshua was an Ephraimite, and the tribe's pride and power made it the leading tribe of the north: after the kingdom divided, 'Ephraim' became shorthand for the whole northern kingdom, and the prophets use the name that way (Hosea 7:8). Samaria, the northern capital, stood in Ephraim's hills. The kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC.
Culture: Ephraim's culture was that of the central highlands: hill farming, the sanctuary at Shiloh, and the political weight of the largest and most influential northern tribe.
Religion: Ephraim shared Israel's worship of the LORD, centred first on the tabernacle at Shiloh, but after the division its kings set up rival sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan, which the prophets condemned.
BibleConnection: Ephraim embodies the younger son chosen over the elder — and the northern kingdom's rise and fall: from Joshua's tribe to Hosea's wayward namesake, still addressed by God as 'my dear son' (Jeremiah 31:20).
KeyScriptures: Genesis 41:52; Genesis 48:17-20; Joshua 16:5-10; Judges 8:1-3; 1 Kings 12:25; Hosea 7:8
RelatedPeople: Ephraim; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Manasseh; Moses; Joshua; Samuel; Deborah; Jeroboam; Abdon, Son of Hillel
RelatedEvents: The Kingdom Divides; Fall of Samaria

Region: East of the Jordan, Gilead from the Arnon to the Jabbok
History: Gad was Jacob's seventh son, by Leah's servant Zilpah. Jacob blessed him as a troop that would be raided and would raid in return (Genesis 49:19). Like Reuben, Gad asked Moses for Transjordan pasture land (Numbers 32) and settled Gilead. Gadites were famed as warriors: eleven Gadite captains joined David in the wilderness (1 Chronicles 12:8-15), and Gad's territory bore the brunt of Syrian and Ammonite attacks. The Mesha Stele, Moab's own record, says Gad had long dwelt in the land of Ataroth. Gad was deported with the other Transjordan tribes by Tiglath-Pileser (1 Chronicles 5:26).
Culture: Gad's culture was that of a warrior-pastoral frontier tribe, raising flocks in Gilead and manning the eastern border against Moab, Ammon, and Syria.
Religion: Gad shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary across the Jordan; its territory included towns with altars and, later, the worship centres of the east.
BibleConnection: Gad embodies the Transjordan bargain: land east of the Jordan in exchange for fighting alongside the other tribes for Canaan, a bargain its warriors honoured from Moses to David.
RelatedPeople: Gad; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Heber, Son of Gad's House

Region: Central Asia Minor (Galatia)
History: Celtic tribes that invaded Asia Minor settled in the central highlands and gave the region its name; under Rome it became the province of Galatia. Paul evangelised its churches on his missionary journeys and wrote them his sharpest letter.
Culture: Celtic heritage under Greco-Roman rule; by New Testament times the Galatians were Greek-speaking provincials, organised in the churches Paul founded.
Religion: Pagan Celtic and Greek cults before conversion; Paul's letter confronts Galatian believers who were turning back to law-observance as the ground of acceptance with God.
BibleConnection: Paul's letter to the Galatians defends justification by faith alone and is addressed to churches he had visited; the churches of Galatia also contributed to the collection for Jerusalem.

TimePeriod: Conquest era through David's reign, c. 1400-1000 BC
Region: Geshur, east of the Sea of Galilee, bordering Bashan and Aram
History: Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom on Israel's northeastern border. Deuteronomy 3:14 notes that Geshur and Maacath were not driven out, and Joshua 12:5 and 13:13 record them as peoples left among Israel. Geshur became royal kin to David: Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, was the mother of Absalom (2 Samuel 3:3), and after killing Amnon, Absalom fled to Geshur and stayed three years (2 Samuel 13:37-38). Geshur and Aram later took Havoth-jair from Israel (1 Chronicles 2:23). A separate southern group of the same name appears among David's raid targets in 1 Samuel 27:8; whether it is the same people is unclear.
Culture: A small border kingdom, strong enough to shelter a royal fugitive and to intermarry with David's house, but never a great power. Its kings are named individually (Talmai) rather than as a dynasty.
Religion: No distinct Geshurite religion is described; as an Aramean kingdom it shared the religious world of Aram.
BibleConnection: Geshur gave David a wife and Absalom a refuge, tying Israel's royal house to the Aramean borderlands and shaping the rebellion that followed.
KeyScriptures: Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 12:5; Joshua 13:13; 2 Samuel 3:3; 2 Samuel 13:37-38; 1 Chronicles 2:23

TimePeriod: Bronze Age, before and during the conquest
Region: Canaan (their exact territory is not stated in the text)
History: The Girgashites are listed among the sons of Canaan in Genesis 10:16, named in the land promise of Genesis 15:21, counted among the seven nations in Deuteronomy 7:1, and named among the peoples to be driven out before Israel in Joshua 3:10 and Joshua 24:11. Beyond these conquest lists, the Bible records nothing more about them: no king, city, or territory is named for them.
Culture: Unknown beyond their place among the Canaanite peoples of the conquest lists.
Religion: Unknown beyond their place among the peoples whose idolatry Israel was told to reject.
BibleConnection: The Girgashites are a reminder of how little the record preserves about some peoples: they are named in every great list of the land's nations, yet leave no story of their own.

Region: Hamath on the Orontes, in Syria
History: The Hamathites, descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:18; 1 Chronicles 1:16), were the people of Hamath, a Syrian kingdom on the Orontes. Hamath's people were among those Assyria resettled in Samaria (2 Kings 17:24), and the kings of Hamath were named by Assyria's king when he mocked the gods of the nations (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13).
Culture: Hamath was an Aramean city-state of farmers and traders on the Orontes, a stopping point between Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean.
Religion: The men of Hamath made Ashima their god (2 Kings 17:30), and carried that worship with them to Samaria.
BibleConnection: Hamath's story in the Bible runs from the Table of Nations to the Assyrian resettlement: a Canaanite people who became a Syrian kingdom and then exiles in Israel's land.

Region: Central and northern Canaan: Shechem, Gibeon, and the region toward Lebanon and Mount Hermon
History: The Hivites are listed among the sons of Canaan in Genesis 10:17. Hamor the Hivite was the prince of Shechem in the Dinah affair (Genesis 34:2). The Gibeonites, who tricked Israel into a covenant in Joshua 9, are identified as Hivites in Joshua 9:7; their cities Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kirjath-jearim were spared and made woodcutters and water drawers for the congregation. They are named among the seven nations in Deuteronomy 7:1 and among the peoples left to test Israel in Judges 3.
Culture: A city-based people of central Canaan. The Gibeonite cities were organized enough to send a delegation and negotiate a treaty, and their servitude in Israel's service lasted for generations.
Religion: They shared the Canaanite religion. The Gibeonites' treaty brought them under Israel's protection, and their service was attached to the sanctuary.
BibleConnection: Hivites appear at two turning points: the violence at Shechem in Jacob's day, and the Gibeonite treaty that taught Israel the cost of a hasty oath in Joshua's day.

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era, before Esau's descendants took Seir
Region: Mount Seir (later Edom) and its mountains
History: The Horites (also called Horim) were the earlier inhabitants of Seir. Chedorlaomer defeated them in Mount Seir in Genesis 14:6, and Genesis 36:20-30 gives the genealogy of Seir the Horite and his sons: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan, the dukes of the Horites. Deuteronomy 2:12 and 2:22 record that the children of Esau destroyed the Horites and dwelt in their stead, just as Israel would later do in Canaan.
Culture: Their name is traditionally connected with cave-dwelling in Seir's mountains. They were organized under dukes, a clan structure that Esau's line inherited along with the land.
Religion: No Horite religion is described in the text.
BibleConnection: The Horites show the pattern Deuteronomy repeats: one people displacing another in the land, so that Edom's story mirrors Israel's own conquest.

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era onward, c. 2000 BC and after
Region: The desert east of Egypt, from Havilah to Shur, and later the northern Arabian desert
History: The Ishmaelites descended from Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar (Genesis 16; 21). Genesis 25:12-18 lists his twelve sons, princes of their tribes, dwelling from Havilah to Shur, east of Egypt. An Ishmaelite caravan carrying spices to Egypt bought Joseph from his brothers (Genesis 37:25-28; the same passage also calls the traders Midianites, and the two names are used together there). Gideon asked for the gold earrings of the Ishmaelite traders after defeating Midian (Judges 8:24), and Psalm 83:6 counts the Ishmaelites among the confederates against Israel.
Culture: Nomadic desert traders, living in tents and moving goods between Arabia and Egypt. Ishmael himself 'grew, and dwelt in the wilderness, and became an archer' (Genesis 21:20).
Religion: The text ties Ishmael's line to Abraham's God through Hagar's encounter at the well (Genesis 16) and God's promise to make Ishmael a great nation (Genesis 17:20), but it describes no distinct Ishmaelite religion.
BibleConnection: Ishmaelites carry Joseph into Egypt, setting the exodus story in motion, and stand as the desert kin of Israel: Abraham's other son's line, blessed yet outside the covenant promise.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 16:11-12; Genesis 21:20-21; Genesis 25:12-18; Genesis 37:25-28; Judges 8:24; Psalm 83:6
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Hagar; Ishmael; Isaac; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; Hagar and Ishmael

Region: Canaan and the land of Israel, eastern Mediterranean coast
History: Israel begins with Jacob, renamed Israel after wrestling with God (Genesis 32). His twelve sons became the twelve tribes. After slavery in Egypt, the Exodus under Moses and the conquest under Joshua gave them the land of Canaan. Under David and Solomon Israel was one kingdom; after Solomon it split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC and Babylon destroyed Judah in 586 BC, but a remnant returned under Cyrus and rebuilt Jerusalem and the temple. In the New Testament the name Israel still denotes God's covenant people, and Paul wrestles with Israel's place in God's purposes in Romans 9–11.
Culture: Israelite culture was built around the family, the tribe, and the covenant law given at Sinai. Agriculture, shepherding, and later town life shaped daily existence; festivals at the tabernacle and then the temple marked the year, and the law governed worship, justice, and neighbourly life.
Religion: Israel worshipped the LORD alone, in contrast to the many gods of its neighbours. The covenant at Sinai, the sacrificial system, the priesthood, and the prophets' call to justice and exclusive loyalty to God define its religion. Idolatry and the worship of Baal and other gods are presented throughout the history as the recurring breach of that covenant.
BibleConnection: Israel is the central people of the whole Bible: the Old Testament is largely their story, and the New Testament presents Jesus as Israel's Messiah, born of Judah, and the church as grafted into Israel's covenant promises.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 32:28; Genesis 35:10; Exodus 19:5-6; Deuteronomy 7:6-8; 1 Kings 12:16-20; 2 Kings 17:6; Ezra 1:1-4; Romans 9:4-5
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Miriam; Joshua; Samuel; Ezra; Nehemiah; Jesus
RelatedPlaces: Canaan; Egypt; Goshen; Jericho; Jerusalem; Samaria; Babylon; Mount Sinai; Jordan River
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Ten Commandments; Crossing the Jordan; The Walls of Jericho; The Kingdom Divides; Fall of Samaria; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Ezra Reads the Law; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple
RelatedFinds: Merneptah Stele; Tel Dan Stele (House of David); Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III; Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III; Cyrus Cylinder; Jehoiachin's Rations Tablets

Region: The Jezreel Valley, south of Naphtali
History: Issachar was Jacob's ninth son, by Leah. Jacob blessed him as a strong donkey crouching between sheepfolds, a tribe that would bear burdens (Genesis 49:14-15). His allotment lay in the fertile Jezreel Valley, including Jezreel and Shunem. Issachar's princes fought with Deborah and Barak (Judges 5:15), and the tribe's later fame was for wisdom: the men of Issachar 'had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do' (1 Chronicles 12:32). Issachar was deported with the northern kingdom.
Culture: Issachar's culture was agricultural: the rich valley soil made it one of Israel's breadbaskets, and its strength lay in farming and in counsel rather than in kings or judges.
Religion: Issachar shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary and later the temple at Jerusalem.
BibleConnection: Issachar is remembered for discernment rather than power: a tribe that knew its times and counselled the nation, in contrast to the strong-man history of its neighbours.
RelatedPeople: Issachar; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Tola, Son of Puah; Baasha, King of Israel

Region: Jerusalem (called Jebus) and its surroundings
History: The Jebusites were the pre-Israelite inhabitants of Jerusalem. Genesis 10:16 lists them among the sons of Canaan. In Judges 1:21 the Benjamites failed to drive them out of Jerusalem, and in Judges 19:10 the city is still called Jebus, a city of the Jebusites. David captured their stronghold, the strong hold of Zion, and made it his capital (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Later, Araunah the Jebusite sold David the threshingfloor on Mount Moriah where the altar was built (2 Samuel 24:18-25).
Culture: A fortified city people. Their stronghold on the hill later called Zion held out against Judah and Benjamin until David took it, and the city they built became the capital of Israel.
Religion: They shared the Canaanite religion of their neighbors. The Bible records no distinct Jebusite cult, only that their city and its threshingfloor passed into Israel's worship when David built an altar there.
BibleConnection: The Jebusites held the city that became Jerusalem. Their defeat gave David his capital, and Araunah's threshingfloor became the site of the future temple.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 10:16; Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21; Judges 19:10; 2 Samuel 5:6-9; 2 Samuel 24:18-25
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Region: Southern hill country, from Jerusalem to Beersheba
History: Judah was Jacob's fourth son by Leah, whose name means praise. Jacob's blessing gave Judah the sceptre and the ruler's staff (Genesis 49:10), and the tribe produced the house of David. Judah's allotment covered the southern hill country including Hebron and, later, Jerusalem. After Solomon's death Judah became the southern kingdom, with Jerusalem and the temple, and it outlasted the northern kingdom by over a century before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC. The returning exiles were largely Judahites, and from 'Judah' comes the name 'Jew'. Jesus was born of Judah, of David's line, in Bethlehem.
Culture: Judah's culture was centred on Jerusalem, the temple, and the Davidic court. Its towns included Hebron, Bethlehem, and Lachish, and its people were farmers, shepherds, and traders of the southern hills.
Religion: Judah's religion was temple religion: sacrifice, priesthood, and the festivals in Jerusalem, guarded by prophets who called kings and people back to the covenant. After the exile, Judah's community rebuilt temple worship and the law became central to Jewish life.
BibleConnection: Judah carries the Bible's central thread: the promise of a ruler from Judah runs from Genesis 49 through David to Jesus, called the Lion of the tribe of Judah in Revelation 5.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 29:35; Genesis 49:8-12; Numbers 2:3; Joshua 15:1; 2 Samuel 2:4; 1 Kings 12:16-20; 2 Kings 25:1-2; Matthew 1:2-3
RelatedPeople: Judah; Jacob; Caleb; Boaz; Ruth; Naomi; Elimelech; King David; King Solomon; Rehoboam; King Asa; King Jehoshaphat; King Hezekiah; King Josiah; Zerubbabel; Jesse; Othniel, Son of Kenaz; Amos; Micah
RelatedEvents: Judah and Tamar; David Becomes King; Building of Solomon's Temple; The Kingdom Divides; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
