Region: The east (the name means 'easterners'); no territory is stated in the text
History: The Kadmonites are named only once in the Bible, in the land promise to Abram (Genesis 15:19), among the peoples of the land: Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaim, Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites. Nothing more is recorded about them: no king, city, territory, or later mention appears anywhere in the text.
Culture: Unknown. Their name points east, and they are sometimes grouped with the 'children of the east' of the desert fringe, but the text itself says no more.
Religion: Unknown.
BibleConnection: The Kadmonites appear only in the promise itself: part of the land God pledged to Abram's descendants, named once and never heard from again.

Region: The Negev and the southern wilderness, associated with Midian and with Judah's southern border
History: The Kenites are named in the land promise of Genesis 15:19 and in Balaam's oracle, which pictures their nest set in the rock (Numbers 24:21). The children of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with Judah into the wilderness of Judah (Judges 1:16), and Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites when his wife Jael killed Sisera (Judges 4:11, 17-22). Saul warned the Kenites to leave the Amalekites before his campaign, because they had shown kindness to Israel coming out of Egypt (1 Samuel 15:6). David shared spoil with the Kenites (1 Samuel 30:29), and 1 Chronicles 2:55 counts scribal families among the Kenites, including the house of Rechab, whose abstinent rule Jeremiah 35 praises.
Culture: The name is traditionally connected with metalworking (Hebrew qayin, 'smith'), and the Kenites lived as tent-dwellers on the desert fringe, at home among both Midian and Judah. The Rechabites kept Jonadab's rule: no wine, no houses, no sown fields.
Religion: Jethro's family acknowledged the LORD (Exodus 18), and the Rechabites' obedience to their ancestor's command is held up in Jeremiah 35 as a rebuke to Judah's disobedience.
BibleConnection: Kenites are Israel's desert friends: kin by marriage to Moses, allies who showed kindness at the exodus, and the people whose tent Jael's peg ended Sisera's army.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 15:19; Numbers 24:21; Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11; Judges 4:17-22; 1 Samuel 15:6; 1 Chronicles 2:55; Jeremiah 35:6-10

Region: Southern Canaan and the Negev, associated with Caleb's family
History: The Kenizzites are named in the land promise of Genesis 15:19 and nowhere else as a nation. Their fame comes through one man: Caleb, son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite (Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:6), who followed the LORD fully and received Hebron as his inheritance. Though called a Kenizzite, Caleb was counted with the tribe of Judah. Kenaz, named in 1 Chronicles 4:13-15, belongs to the same family line, and Othniel son of Kenaz took Debir and became a judge.
Culture: Little is recorded beyond their place in the Genesis 15 list and Caleb's line. They appear as a southern clan absorbed into Judah rather than as a separate kingdom.
Religion: No distinct Kenizzite religion is described. Caleb's faithfulness is the family's mark in the text.
BibleConnection: Through Caleb the Kenizzite, this obscure people of the promise list produced one of Israel's great heroes of faith, the spy who believed God could give the land.

Region: No single territory; 48 cities scattered throughout Israel
History: Levi was Jacob's third son by Leah, and with Simeon he shared in the Shechem violence (Genesis 34). The tribe was set apart after the golden calf, when the Levites rallied to Moses (Exodus 32:26-29). Levi received no tribal territory; instead the Levites were given 48 cities scattered among the other tribes (Joshua 21) and lived from the tithes, serving the tabernacle and later the temple. Aaron's descendants were the priests; the other Levites assisted them. Moses, Aaron, and Miriam were all Levites. Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16) was a Levite challenge to Aaron's priesthood.
Culture: Levite culture was defined by service rather than land: teaching the law, assisting at sacrifices, singing and guarding the sanctuary, and living dispersed among the other tribes as their religious instructors.
Religion: The Levites embodied Israel's priestly religion: Aaron's sons offered the sacrifices, and the tribe as a whole maintained the sanctuary, taught the law, and modelled the claim that the LORD himself was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20).
BibleConnection: Levi's blessing in Deuteronomy 33 praises the tribe that taught God's law and kept his covenant. In the New Testament the Levites appear in the parable of the good Samaritan and in the temple service that frames Jesus' ministry.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 29:34; Genesis 49:5-7; Exodus 32:26-29; Numbers 3:5-13; Numbers 18:20-24; Joshua 21:1-3; Deuteronomy 33:8-11
RelatedPeople: Levi; Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Miriam; Eleazar; Phinehas; Ithamar; Nadab; Abihu; Eli; Samuel; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Ten Commandments

Region: North Africa, west of Egypt
History: The Lubim, or Libyans, appear as warriors of the North African coast west of Egypt. They marched with Shishak against Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 12:3) and are named among Egypt's allies (2 Chronicles 16:8; Nahum 3:9). Ezekiel lists Libya among the peoples falling with Egypt (Ezekiel 30:5) and among Gog's allies (Ezekiel 38:5), and Libyans were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). The Lehabim of Genesis 10:13 are traditionally identified with these Libyans.
Culture: Libyans were semi-nomadic herders and warriors of the coastal tribes, serving as soldiers and charioteers in Egyptian and other Near Eastern armies.
Religion: Libyans shared much of Egypt's religious world, worshipping Libyan and Egyptian deities of the desert and the Nile valley.
BibleConnection: Libya's biblical role is chiefly as Egypt's western neighbor and ally, named in judgment oracles and, at Pentecost, among the nations hearing the gospel in their own tongue.
KeyScriptures: 2 Chronicles 12:3; 2 Chronicles 16:8; Nahum 3:9; Ezekiel 30:5; Ezekiel 38:5; Acts 2:10

Region: Interior Asia Minor (Lycaonia)
History: Lycaonia was an inland district of Asia Minor. Paul preached at Lystra and Derbe in Lycaonia, where the crowds, hearing him in their own language, cried out that the gods had come down in human form and tried to sacrifice to him and Barnabas.
Culture: Lycaonian speech survived alongside Greek in a rural, pastoral district.
Religion: Local Zeus and Hermes cults — the crowd took Barnabas for Zeus and Paul for Hermes — before the gospel reached them.
BibleConnection: The Lycaonians' reaction at Lystra, and Paul's stoning there and return, are the Lycaonians' main New Testament appearance.

Region: Western Asia Minor (modern Turkey), around Sardis
History: Lud, son of Shem (Genesis 10:22), is the ancestor of the Lydians, whose kingdom in western Asia Minor grew rich on trade and is traditionally credited with the first coined money. Under kings such as Alyattes and Croesus the kingdom flourished until Cyrus of Persia conquered it in 546 BC. In the prophets, Lud's bowmen serve Tyre and fall with Egypt's allies.
Culture: Lydians were traders and craftsmen, famed for textiles, dyes, and gold from the Pactolus river, and for an early coinage that spread across the ancient world.
Religion: Lydians worshipped Anatolian deities, including the mother goddess Cybele, alongside Greek and Near Eastern gods of the region.
BibleConnection: Lydia appears as Lud among the nations in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre (Ezekiel 27:10), among the peoples falling with Egypt (Ezekiel 30:5), and among the nations to which escapees are sent (Isaiah 66:19). The Lydia of Acts 16 is a different matter: she is an individual woman from Thyatira, not the nation, and is not cited here.

TimePeriod: Conquest era through the divided monarchy
Region: Maacah, northeast of Bashan, bordering Geshur
History: Maacah was a small kingdom northeast of Bashan. Like Geshur, it was not driven out in the conquest (Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 13:13), and Joshua 12:5 marks it on the border of Og's kingdom. In David's wars the king of Maacah sent a thousand men to fight with the Ammonites against Israel (2 Samuel 10:6, 8). Eliphelet, son of Ahasbai the Maachathite, served among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:34), and Jaazaniah the Maachathite was among the captains who came to Gedaliah after Jerusalem's fall (Jeremiah 40:8).
Culture: A small border people, able to field troops for a coalition war yet small enough that its men served individually in David's and Gedaliah's companies.
Religion: No distinct Maacathite religion is described.
BibleConnection: Maacah appears at both ends of the monarchy: fighting David with Ammon, then standing with Gedaliah's remnant after the exile began.
KeyScriptures: Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 12:5; Joshua 13:13; 2 Samuel 10:6; 2 Samuel 23:34; Jeremiah 40:8

Region: Both sides of the Jordan: central hill country west, and Bashan and Gilead east
History: Manasseh was Joseph's elder son, adopted by Jacob as a tribal ancestor alongside Ephraim (Genesis 48). The tribe was the only one besides Reuben and Gad to hold land on both sides of the Jordan: half settled the central hills west of the river, and half took Bashan and northern Gilead east of it (Joshua 17; Numbers 32:33-42). Gideon, who delivered Israel from Midian, was a Manassite of Abiezer (Judges 6:15), and the judge Jephthah was a Gileadite. Manasseh's eastern half was deported early by Assyria, and the western half fell with Samaria in 722 BC.
Culture: Manasseh's culture was split by the Jordan: hill farming in the west, and pastoral, frontier life in Bashan and Gilead in the east, where its warriors guarded Israel's northern border.
Religion: Manasseh shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary at Shiloh and later the temple, though its eastern towns lived far from both.
BibleConnection: Manasseh's double territory made it a bridge tribe: its western half gave the north its heartland, its eastern half its frontier, and its Gideon gave Israel one of its greatest deliverers.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 41:51; Genesis 48:13-20; Numbers 26:28-34; Joshua 17:1-6; Numbers 32:33-42; Judges 6:15
RelatedPeople: Manasseh; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Ephraim; Moses; Joshua; Gideon; Jephthah, Judge of Israel; Jair, the Gileadite; Zelophehad
RelatedEvents: Gideon's Victory over Midian; Fall of Samaria

Region: Northwestern Iran, south of the Caspian Sea
History: The Medes were an Iranian people whose kingdom, under kings such as Cyaxares, joined Babylon in destroying Nineveh in 612 BC. Cyrus of Persia conquered Media around 550 BC, and the two peoples formed the Medo-Persian Empire, whose law was famously unchangeable (Daniel 6:8). Darius the Mede took Babylon after its fall and ruled it while Daniel served at court.
Culture: Medes were famed as horsemen and warriors, and their court dress and customs deeply influenced the Persian Empire that absorbed them.
Religion: The Medes practiced an early form of Iranian religion; later tradition connects their priestly class, the magi, with Zoroastrian teaching, though the text itself does not describe their worship.
BibleConnection: The Medes are God's named instrument against Babylon (Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11, 28), and Daniel's career spans their rule: the lions' den is dated to Darius the Mede, and Daniel's vision of the ram names the two horns as the kings of Media and Persia (Daniel 8:20).
KeyScriptures: Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11; Daniel 5:28; Daniel 6:8; Daniel 8:20; Daniel 9:1; Acts 2:9
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Pentecost

Region: Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and Euphrates
History: Mesopotamia was the land between the rivers, Abraham's homeland. Dwellers in Mesopotamia are named among the hearers at Pentecost, and Stephen recalls God appearing to Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia.
Culture: Ancient cities, Aramaic-speaking under Parthian rule, with a large Jewish diaspora.
Religion: Old Mesopotamian cults alongside a strong Jewish diaspora community.
BibleConnection: Named at Pentecost, and named again as Abraham's homeland in Stephen's speech.

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era through the judges, c. 2000-1100 BC
Region: East of the Gulf of Aqaba, the Sinai wilderness, and Transjordan (northwest Arabia)
History: The Midianites descended from Midian, son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Moses fled to Midian after killing the Egyptian, married Zipporah, daughter of Jethro the priest of Midian, and met God at the burning bush there (Exodus 2-3). Midian joined Moab in hiring Balaam (Numbers 22) and in the Baal-peor affair (Numbers 25), for which Israel made war on Midian (Numbers 31). In Gideon's day the Midianites, with Amalek and the children of the east, oppressed Israel for seven years until Gideon's three hundred routed them (Judges 6-8).
Culture: Nomadic herders and caravan traders of the desert fringe, living in tents and moving with their flocks. Their caravans linked Arabia, Egypt, and Canaan, and their kings are named in the Gideon campaign (Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, Zalmunna).
Religion: Midianite religion included Baal-peor, worshipped with Moab in Numbers 25. Yet Jethro, priest of Midian, is shown acknowledging the LORD and offering sacrifice with Moses and Aaron (Exodus 18).
BibleConnection: Midian is where Moses found refuge, a wife, and his calling; and where Gideon won his great victory. The Midianite caravan also carried Joseph toward Egypt (Genesis 37:28, where the traders are called both Midianites and Ishmaelites).
KeyScriptures: Genesis 25:2; Exodus 2:15-21; Exodus 18:1-12; Numbers 25:16-18; Numbers 31:1-12; Judges 6:1-6; Judges 7:19-25
RelatedPeople: Moses; Jethro; Hobab; Gideon; Midian; Keturah; Zipporah; Reuel
RelatedEvents: Gideon's Victory over Midian; Joseph and His Brothers; The Burning Bush

Region: Upper Galilee, west of the Jordan's sources
History: Naphtali was Jacob's sixth son, by Rachel's servant Bilhah. Jacob blessed him as a hind let loose (Genesis 49:21). His tribe settled the hills of Upper Galilee, around Kedesh. Barak, who defeated Sisera with Deborah, mustered his army from Naphtali (Judges 4:6), and Naphtali's men are praised for risking their lives in the battle (Judges 5:18). The tribe was among the first deported by Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Isaiah's promise that a light would dawn on 'the land of Naphtali' (Isaiah 9:1-2) is applied to Jesus' ministry in Galilee in Matthew 4.
Culture: Naphtali's culture was that of the Galilean hills: farming, herding, and the fortified towns of the north, on the frontier with Syria and Phoenicia.
Religion: Naphtali shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary and later the temple, and its towns included Kedesh, a city of refuge.
BibleConnection: Naphtali links Deborah's victory to Jesus' ministry: the same northern hills where Barak fought are where Isaiah promised light and where Jesus began preaching.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 30:8; Genesis 49:21; Deuteronomy 33:23; Judges 4:6; Judges 5:18; 2 Kings 15:29; Isaiah 9:1-2; Matthew 4:13-16
RelatedPeople: Naphtali; Jacob; Deborah; Barak; Jael; Moses; Joshua

TimePeriod: Before the Flood, and again in the wilderness generation (as reported)
Region: No territory is given for them
History: The Nephilim are named twice. Genesis 6:4 says, 'There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.' Numbers 13:33 reports the spies' words: 'we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers.' Whether the Nephilim of Genesis 6 are the same as the Anakim of Numbers 13 is debated; this entry records both passages without merging them into a settled identification.
Culture: The text gives no culture for them beyond great stature and renown, set against the wickedness of the age before the Flood.
Religion: None is described. Their story belongs to the corruption that preceded the Flood, not to any nation's worship.
BibleConnection: The Nephilim frame the Bible's two great judgments on giants: the wickedness before the Flood, and the fear that nearly turned Israel back at the edge of the promised land.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Region: Southern coast of Asia Minor (Pamphylia)
History: Pamphylia was the coastal plain of southern Asia Minor. Pamphylians are named among the hearers at Pentecost; Paul landed at Perga in Pamphylia on his first journey, and John Mark left the party there.
Culture: Greek coastal cities under Roman rule, with the temple of Artemis at Perga among their landmarks.
Religion: Pagan temples before conversion; Paul preached in the region on his first journey.
BibleConnection: Named among the Pentecost hearers; Paul's first journey passed through Pamphylia twice, landing at Perga and later returning through it.

Region: Persia and Mesopotamia east of Rome
History: Parthia was the Iranian empire east of Rome, its great eastern rival. Parthians are named among the hearers at Pentecost; the New Testament says nothing further about them.
Culture: A horse-archer aristocracy ruling a Greek-influenced administration across Persia and Mesopotamia.
Religion: Zoroastrian tradition alongside other cults of the empire.
BibleConnection: Named only in the Acts 2 list of peoples who heard the apostles at Pentecost.

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era through the conquest, c. 2000-1200 BC
Region: The hill country and open country of Canaan, especially around Shechem and Bethel
History: The Perizzites appear in the land from Abram's time: in Genesis 13:7 the Canaanite and the Perizzite already dwelt in the land when Abram and Lot separated. They are named in the promise of Genesis 15:20, in the exodus promise of Exodus 3:8, and among the seven nations of Deuteronomy 7:1. In Joshua 17:15 Joshua tells the house of Joseph to clear land in the hill country of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, and in Judges 1:4-5 Judah defeated the Perizzites at Bezek.
Culture: Their name is often connected with unwalled villages and open country, in contrast to the fortified cities of other Canaanite peoples. They lived alongside the Canaanites in the hill country rather than in one great city.
Religion: The text gives no distinct Perizzite religion; they are counted among the peoples whose idolatry Israel was told to reject.
BibleConnection: Perizzites stand in the background of the whole story, from Abram's arrival to the conquest: one of the peoples already in the land when God promised it, and one of the peoples Israel was told to displace.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 13:7; Genesis 15:20; Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 7:1; Joshua 17:15; Judges 1:4-5

Region: West-central Asia Minor (Phrygia)
History: Phrygia had been an ancient kingdom famed in legend for King Midas; by New Testament times it was part of the Roman province of Asia. Phrygians are named among the hearers at Pentecost, and Paul crossed Phrygia on his journeys.
Culture: Phrygian speech and the old mother-goddess cults were giving way to Greek language and Roman ways.
Religion: The mother-goddess cult before conversion; Christian communities grew along Paul's routes.
BibleConnection: Named among the Pentecost hearers; Paul passed through Phrygia and Galatia on his second journey and through Galatia and Phrygia on his third.

Region: Black Sea coast of Asia Minor (Pontus)
History: Pontus, on the southern Black Sea coast, had been a kingdom and was a Roman province by New Testament times. Pontians are named among the hearers at Pentecost, and Peter addresses his first letter to believers in Pontus.
Culture: Greek coastal cities with an inland population, under Roman administration.
Religion: Pagan cults before conversion; Christian communities existed there by the time of 1 Peter.
BibleConnection: Named among the Pentecost hearers; Aquila, Paul's fellow worker, was a native of Pontus; 1 Peter is addressed in part to Pontus.

Region: North Africa, west of Egypt (the Libya region)
History: Put, son of Ham (Genesis 10:6), is a North African people closely linked with the Libyans. The King James Version spells the name Phut in Genesis and Ezekiel and Put in Nahum. Put's warriors served in Tyre's army (Ezekiel 27:10), stood with Egypt's allies (Ezekiel 30:5; Nahum 3:9), and are named among Gog's coalition (Ezekiel 38:5). Beyond this warrior role, little is recorded of them.
Culture: Like their Libyan neighbors, the men of Put were known as soldiers and mercenaries in the armies of Tyre, Egypt, and the great powers.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Put's religion; as a North African people they shared the religious world of Libya and Egypt.
BibleConnection: Put appears only as a military ally in the prophets — with Tyre, with Egypt, and with Gog — a small people named wherever the great powers mustered their armies.

TimePeriod: Bronze Age, from Genesis 14 to David's reign
Region: Bashan (Og's kingdom), the Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem, and Transjordan
History: The Rephaim were a people of great stature, remembered as giants. Chedorlaomer defeated them at Ashteroth Karnaim (Genesis 14:5), and they are named in the promise of Genesis 15:20. Deuteronomy 2 explains that the Emim and the Zamzummim were also accounted Rephaim, and that Og king of Bashan was 'of the remnant of the giants' (Deuteronomy 3:11), his iron bedstead kept at Rabbath as a curiosity. Joshua 12:4 and 13:12 record Og's kingdom as the last Rephaim territory, and David fought Philistines in the Valley of Rephaim (2 Samuel 5:18-22). Later Philistine giants (2 Samuel 21:16-22) are described as sons of Rapha, linking them to this giant tradition.
Culture: Remembered above all for their stature: 'a people great, and many, and tall' (Deuteronomy 2:10). They held kingdoms and valleys that Israel inherited piece by piece.
Religion: The text describes no Rephaim religion. In later biblical usage the same word shades into 'the shades' of the dead, but the people of Bashan and the valley are a nation, not a ghost story.
BibleConnection: The Rephaim are the giants of the conquest story: the fear behind the spies' report, the kingdom of Og that fell before Israel, and the valley where David fought for Jerusalem.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 14:5; Genesis 15:20; Deuteronomy 2:10-11; Deuteronomy 3:11; Joshua 12:4; 2 Samuel 5:18-22
RelatedPeople: Og; Abraham; Moses; King David; Joshua

Region: East of the Jordan, from the Arnon to Heshbon
History: Reuben was Jacob's firstborn, by Leah, but he lost the birthright after sleeping with his father's concubine Bilhah (Genesis 35:22; 49:3-4). At the settlement the tribe asked Moses for the pasture land east of the Jordan, on condition its fighting men cross over to help conquer Canaan (Numbers 32). Reubenites Dathan and Abiram joined Korah's rebellion against Moses (Numbers 16). The tribe was among the first carried away when Assyria overran the east-Jordan territory under Tiglath-Pileser (1 Chronicles 5:26).
Culture: Reuben shared the pastoral, tribal culture of Israel east of the Jordan, raising flocks on the Transjordan plateau. Its towns included Heshbon, a former Amorite capital, and its territory bordered Moab.
Religion: Reuben shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the tabernacle and later the temple at Jerusalem, despite living across the Jordan from them.
BibleConnection: Reuben's story is a warning about the firstborn's lost privilege: Jacob's blessing says Reuben was 'unstable as water' and would not excel. The tribe's request for land east of the Jordan set the pattern for the two and a half Transjordan tribes.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 29:32; Genesis 35:22; Genesis 49:3-4; Numbers 32:1-5; Joshua 13:15-23; Numbers 16:1
RelatedPeople: Reuben; Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Eleazar; Phinehas; Dathan; Abiram
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Crossing the Jordan

Region: Samaria, between Judea and Galilee
History: After Assyria conquered the northern kingdom, the population of Samaria mixed Israelite remnants with settlers from elsewhere in the empire. By New Testament times the Samaritans were a distinct people with their own temple on Mount Gerizim and a long, bitter estrangement from the Jews.
Culture: Samaritans kept the Torah (in their own Samaritan Pentateuch), observed the Sabbath and the feasts, and worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem.
Religion: Samaritan religion centred on the God of Israel, the Torah, Mount Gerizim as the chosen place of worship, and the expectation of a prophet like Moses (John 4:25).
BibleConnection: Jesus made a Samaritan the hero of his parable of neighbour-love, spoke at length with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, praised a Samaritan leper's thanks, and sent Philip to preach in Samaria, where Samaritans believed and received the Holy Spirit.
KeyScriptures: Matthew 10:5; Luke 10:33; Luke 17:16; John 4:9; Acts 8:25; 2 Kings 17:29; John 4:39

Region: Steppe north of the Black Sea
History: Scythians were the nomadic steppe peoples north of the Black Sea, proverbial outsiders in the Greek world. Paul names them once, as the far edge of the distinctions abolished in Christ.
Culture: Nomadic horsemen and famed archers, outside the Greek and Jewish worlds alike.
Religion: Steppe gods and customs, far from temple or synagogue.
BibleConnection: Named once, in Paul's list of distinctions — Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, Barbarian, Scythian — that do not divide those renewed in Christ.

Region: Sepharvaim, on the Euphrates in Mesopotamia
History: Sepharvaim was one of the Mesopotamian peoples Assyria resettled in Samaria after Israel's fall (2 Kings 17:24). The Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim (2 Kings 17:31), and the kings of Sepharvaim were named by Assyria's king when he mocked the gods of the nations (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13).
Culture: As a Mesopotamian people, the Sepharvites shared the urban culture of the Euphrates cities.
Religion: The Sepharvites worshipped Adrammelech and Anammelech, to whom they offered child sacrifice — the Bible's darkest note on their religion.
BibleConnection: Sepharvaim stands in the Bible as a warning example twice over: a people whose gods could not save their cities from Assyria, and whose worship in Samaria showed how far the resettled land had fallen.

Region: Southwestern Arabia (modern Yemen)
History: Sheba, the Sabaean kingdom of southwestern Arabia, grew wealthy on the frankincense and myrrh trade. Its queen visited Solomon to test his wisdom and left laden with gifts (1 Kings 10). Sabeans raided Job's livestock (Job 1:15), Sheba's merchants traded with Tyre (Ezekiel 27:22), and the prophets picture Sheba's gold and incense coming to Jerusalem (Psalms 72:10; Isaiah 60:6).
Culture: Sabaeans built an irrigation civilization around the Marib dam, carved inscriptions in their own South Arabian script, and ran caravans carrying incense, spices, gold, and precious stones across Arabia.
Religion: Sabaeans worshipped astral deities, chief among them the moon god Almaqah and a sun goddess, with temples and offerings tied to their irrigation state.
BibleConnection: Sheba's queen is the Bible's great example of a foreign ruler seeking Israel's wisdom, and Jesus pointed to her — the queen of the south — as a witness against his own generation (Matthew 12:42).
KeyScriptures: Genesis 10:28; 1 Kings 10:1; Job 1:15; Psalms 72:10; Isaiah 60:6; Ezekiel 27:22; Matthew 12:42

Region: The Negev within Judah's allotment, around Beersheba
History: Simeon was Jacob's second son by Leah. With his brother Levi he avenged Dinah by killing the men of Shechem (Genesis 34), and Jacob's blessing scattered both brothers in Israel (Genesis 49:5-7). Simeon's allotment lay inside Judah's territory in the south (Joshua 19:1-9), and the tribe was gradually absorbed into Judah; Simeonites are still named among those who joined Hezekiah's and Josiah's reforms (2 Chronicles 15:9; 34:6). By the second census the tribe had already shrunk sharply (Numbers 26:14).
Culture: Simeon shared Judah's southern, semi-pastoral culture, living in Negev towns such as Beersheba among Judah's settlements rather than as a separate territorial power.
Religion: Simeon shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with no separate cult or priesthood of its own; its towns fell under Judah's religious life centred on Jerusalem.
BibleConnection: Simeon's history illustrates Jacob's blessing fulfilled literally: a tribe scattered within Israel rather than holding its own land, yet still counted among the twelve and named in the sealing of Revelation 7.
RelatedPeople: Simeon; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Zimri, Son of Salu; Shaul

Region: Canaan (location uncertain)
History: The Sinites are named once in the Table of Nations as descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:17; 1 Chronicles 1:15), with no further biblical history. Later writers proposed locations from the northern Levant to farther east, but the text itself gives no location and no story, and none of those identifications is settled.
Culture: Nothing is recorded of Sinite culture apart from their place in the Canaanite family list.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Sinite religion; as Canaanites they belonged to the wider Canaanite world.
BibleConnection: The Sinites matter here only as part of the Bible's own map of the peoples: one branch of Canaan's family, named and then never heard from again.

Region: Phoenician coast under Syria
History: Syrophoenicia was the Phoenician coast as part of the Roman province of Syria. A Syrophoenician woman sought Jesus for her demon-possessed daughter, and he praised her faith; Mark names her people explicitly, 'a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation.'
Culture: Phoenician cities, Greek-speaking under Roman Syria.
Religion: Pagan background; the woman's persistence and faith are the story's point.
BibleConnection: Mark is the only Gospel to name this people, and he does so precisely to mark the woman as an outsider to Israel whose faith Jesus honoured.

Region: The land later held by Ammon, east of the Jordan
History: The Zamzummim were an ancient people of the Ammonite country, remembered as giants. Deuteronomy 2:20-21 says their land 'also was accounted a land of giants: giants dwelt therein in old time; and the Ammonites call them Zamzummim; a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they succeeded them.' The Zuzim defeated at Ham in Genesis 14:5 are commonly identified with the Zamzummim, the same people under an older name.
Culture: Known only as a great and tall people, counted among the Rephaim, whose land passed to Ammon.
Religion: Not described in the text.
BibleConnection: Like the Emim, the Zamzummim teach Deuteronomy's point: God gave Ammon its land by displacing giants, just as He gave Israel Canaan.

Region: Lower Galilee, between the Jezreel Valley and the coast
History: Zebulun was Jacob's tenth son, by Leah. Jacob blessed him as a haven for ships (Genesis 49:13), though his allotment in Lower Galilee never quite reached the sea. Zebulun's men fought with Deborah and Barak and are praised for risking their lives on the heights (Judges 5:18); the tribe also supplied Elon, one of the minor judges (Judges 12:11-12). Isaiah's promise of light to Zebulun and Naphtali (Isaiah 9:1) is applied to Jesus' Galilean ministry in Matthew 4. Zebulun was deported with the northern kingdom.
Culture: Zebulun's culture was that of the Galilean farming towns, trading toward the coast and the great north-south road, with a reputation for loyalty in battle disproportionate to its size.
Religion: Zebulun shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary and later the temple.
BibleConnection: Zebulun links the judges' battlefield to the Gospels: the tribe praised for risking its life at the Kishon is named in the same Isaiah promise that Matthew applies to Jesus in Galilee.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 30:20; Genesis 49:13; Deuteronomy 33:18-19; Joshua 19:10-16; Judges 5:14; Isaiah 9:1
RelatedPeople: Zebulun; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Deborah; Barak; Elon, Judge of Israel

Region: Canaan (later Sumur on the Phoenician coast is the proposed identification)
History: The Zemarites are named in the Table of Nations as descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:18; 1 Chronicles 1:16), with no further biblical history. The later coastal town of Sumur (Simyra) in the northern Levant has been proposed as their place, but the text itself does not say so, and the identification remains a proposal, not a certainty.
Culture: Nothing is recorded of Zemarite culture apart from their place in the Canaanite family list.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Zemarite religion.
BibleConnection: The Zemarites appear only in the Table of Nations, one branch of Canaan's family spread abroad.
